title: Batching + pacing savings hypothesis log
content:
TL;DR:
This note captures a set of hypotheses, measurement approaches, and demo scripts that show how request-level pacing + smart micro-batching and KV/prefix caching produce observable cost reductions for real product workloads while preserving P95 latency SLOs. Goal: give GTM a compact set of reproducible proof points and short scripts reps can use on calls or in proposals.

Why this matters (single-sentence):
Customers buy predictable latency or predictable $$—we show how small runtime controls (pacing window, burst smoothing, per-tenant batch caps) convert into 20–60% token cost reduction for typical interactive completions without increasing perceived latency.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Micro-batching + 10–30ms pacing window yields 25–40% token-cost reduction on interactive chat where median request size <= 800 tokens and inter-arrival times cluster within 50ms bursts.
2) KV/prefix caching amortizes warm-token work for sessionized apps and reduces per-token compute by 15–35% depending on prompt reuse.
3) Combining adaptive pacing (shorter windows at low load, slightly longer when load spikes) preserves P95 latency while capturing batching benefits (wins over static batching policy).
4) For enterprise SLAs that require p95 < 300ms, we can still deliver 15–20% cost improvement via pacing + routing to cheaper model variants for non-critical paths.

Measurement plan (how to prove):
- Data required: trace-level request timestamps, token counts (input/output), model variant used, per-request latency (server and end-to-end), cost per GPU-second or per-token proxy.
- Baseline: measure 2 weeks of live traffic from 3 customer archetypes (support chat, assistive editor, semantic search) under current runtime settings (no pacing).
- Treatment variants: (A) 10ms pacing window micro-batches, (B) 25ms pacing, (C) adaptive pacing (10ms nominal, up to 50ms when burst detected), (D) pacing + prefix caching enabled for session IDs.
- Primary metrics: per-request cost proxy (GPU-ms/token), total tokens served per GPU-hour, p50/p95 latency, % of requests served from cache, throughput (requests/sec).
- Success criteria: >=20% reduction in cost proxy vs baseline with p95 increase <= 10% absolute and p95 <= customer SLA threshold.

Experiment matrix (quick):
- Simulated workload profiles:
  1) Low concurrency, high-len requests (editor: median 1.8k tokens/session).
  2) Chatty micro-interactions (support: median 350 tokens, bursts of 5–10 reqs/sec).
  3) Mixed sessionized (assistant: repeated prefixes, median 700 tokens).
- Run each profile against baseline and A/B treatments for 24-hour windows.

Concrete math examples (for sales scripts) — keep simple, repeatable: 
Example A: chatty support (median request 400 tokens, avg tokens per session 1,600)
- Baseline: 1k sessions = 1.6M tokens -> runtime cost proxy = $X per 1M tokens (use account-level number in pitch; placeholder below).
- With 20ms batching (observed throughput uplift 1.6x), effective cost per token drops ~37% (rough numbers for demo).
- Sales script line: "On your traffic profile this means we typically see 30–40% lower inference spend after enabling micro-batching + cache, with no perceptible delay for end users."

Example B: editor-style (longer prompts, fewer requests)
- Prefix caching helps more: if 40% of tokens are repeated in session prefix, compute work saved ~35% -> overall cost down 15–25%.
- Sales script: "For sessionized editors we can reclaim a big chunk of redundant compute via KV/prefix caching—customers often see 15–25% savings straight away."

Demo scenarios & scripts (engineer-friendly, short):
1) Live demo — microburst smoothing
- Setup: small load generator, 200 concurrent clients, each emits bursts of 3 requests spaced 20ms apart. Baseline run for 10 minutes, then enable 25ms pacing + adaptive routing to cheaper compatible variant for low-importance calls.
- Observable: watch tokens/GPU-hour drop on console, p95 stays within SLA. Powerpoint slide: two charts side-by-side (tokens/GPU-hour, p95 latency).
- Talking points: "Notice how short pacing windows act like a tiny queue that lets us fill GPU work without pushing user-visible delay past the median. We convert tail microbursts into small batches."

2) Customer role-play — cost estimate walk-through
- Script: "We ran your sample for 100k user sessions. With current config you'd spend approx $Y per month. By enabling batching and cache we model a conservative 25% reduction, saving ~$0.25*Y monthly—here's a one-page estimate"

3) Proof-of-value to procurement: SLA + unit economics tie
- Provide two-line guarantee: if p95 latency increases >10% or cost savings <15% in a 30-day POC, Redwood will supply a free optimization engagement (or credit).

Competitive notes (short bullets) — how to position vs major comps: 
- Open-hosted LLM APIs (large provider A): often don't expose batching controls and charge per-token with opaque multi-tenant packing. Our angle: we expose runtime knobs and can guarantee per-tenant isolation + predictable cost improvements via reserved capacity.
- Self-hosted runtimes: may achieve similar savings but require the customer to build orchestration (routing, batching policy, cache invalidation). Our differentiation: turnkey controls, telemetry, and rollout safety (canary + fallbacks).
- Vendor B (specialized inference vendor): may advertise similar batching but usually requires model conversion/quantization steps that can introduce quality regressions. We emphasize measured end-to-end quality checks and quantization-aware routing that preserves logits where needed.

Objections and rebuttals (quick):
- "Batching will add latency to users" -> rebuttal: "We tune pacing to target median effect; micro-windows (10–30ms) are imperceptible for interactive apps and we offer dynamic policies that expand only under load spikes."
- "This sounds like a paper optimization" -> rebuttal: "We have repeatable proofs on three archetypes and an offer to run the customer's trace in our lab to produce a tailored ROI memo in 48–72 hours."

Sales-ready positioning snippets (short):
- Elevator: "Redwood reduces inference spend by capturing batching and cache opportunities in live traffic while protecting latency SLOs — so you get lower TCO without trading away responsiveness."
- Pitch bullet: "Up to ~40% inference spend reduction on chatty workloads via micro-batching + KV caching; predictable P95 latency or our optimization credit."
- For security-conscious customers: "Same savings in Dedicated/Private — applied within your VPC with tenant isolation and no cross-tenant packing."

Operational considerations & risks: 
- Monitoring: need token-level cost attribution, batch occupancy histograms, per-tenant cache hit rates, and sudden-pacing-induced queuing alerts.
- Rollouts: start with canary traffic slice (1–5%), ramp to 25%, then to 100% while tracking p95 and error rates.
- Edge cases: very low-latency single-token streaming (voice assistants) should opt-out of batching; mark via route-level config.

Next steps & short checklist for GTM collateral: 
- Produce a 1-pager ROI calculator template for sales (inputs: median tokens/session, sessions/day, desired SLA).
- Create a short demo deck and one-click lab runbook for solutions engineers (30–60 minute lab).
- Draft a customer-facing POC terms paragraph (commitments, measurement window, success criteria, credit if missed).
- Build two canned dashboards: cost proxy vs baseline and batch occupancy over time.

Open questions (to resolve with applied-ml + runtime):
- Precise default pacing windows by archetype (we need runtime/bench experiments to pick conservative defaults).
- Cost proxy mapping to real $ on Hosted (need finance input to convert GPU-hr to per-token pricing).
- Whether we should expose pacing controls in Console or keep it SRE-managed for early POCs.

Appendix: quick log of preliminary runs (informal notes)
- 2025-01-18: internal bench with webchat trace (500k requests). 25ms pacing gave 32% token-cost proxy reduction; p95 increased from 210ms -> 235ms.
- 2025-01-29: cache-enabled run on same trace saw additional 18% reduction of compute due to repeated prefixes; effective cumulative ~44%.
- 2025-02-05: customer sample (beta customer X) simulated POC: projected monthly savings ~28% at 75% confidence.

Notes-to-self: keep the customer numbers conservative in public materials; use concrete lab outputs for rebuttals.

---
If reviewers want, I can convert this into a 1-slide proof-of-value and a short two-paragraph customer email template.
